name: Houttuynia cordata

lead: Houttuynia cordata, called fish mint or heartleaf, is a herb eaten in East and Southeast Asia and used in traditional medicine. Its extract is common in Korean toners, serums and sheet masks used for calming redness and oily, blemish-prone skin.

The chain is soothing: flavonoids such as quercitrin lower inflammatory mediators and show antioxidant effects in cell studies, and extracts have antibacterial activity against acne bacteria in vitro. The result people want is less visible irritation and blemishing and a clearer, calmer look. Support comes mainly from cell studies and a small reported toner study; controlled skin trials were not found.

paras: Applied as a toner, serum or sheet mask after cleansing, often as the calming step in routines for oily or breakout-prone skin. It is commonly paired with centella, salicylic acid or niacinamide products. Users typically report calmer skin within days to weeks.
Contact dermatitis is reported in sensitive users, and a patch test is the usual advice. Injectable forms have caused severe allergic reactions, and high oral doses were toxic in animal studies.

angle.text: Heartleaf extract is used in Korean toners, serums and sheet masks to calm redness and keep oily, blemish-prone skin looking clearer. Its flavonoids lower inflammatory signals and act against acne bacteria in cell studies, which is the route to less visible irritation.

lead: Houttuynia cordata, called fish mint, heartleaf or chameleon plant, is a perennial native to Southeast Asia used as a vegetable and herb in Vietnam, Japan, Korea, northeastern India and southwestern China, and in traditional Chinese medicine.[1] Its extract, marketed as "heartleaf", is a prominent ingredient in Korean skincare toners, serums and sheet masks.[1][2]

Evidence on skin is mostly laboratory-based; Wikipedia notes there was no high-quality clinical research confirming safety or effectiveness as of 2018.[1] Injectable preparations have caused severe allergic reactions.[1]

paras: The plant grows in moist shady places, spreads by rhizomes and is considered invasive. Its leaves have a fishy taste from the volatile compound decanoyl acetaldehyde.[1] In China it is used for conditions such as pneumonia, abscesses and skin infections in traditional medicine; in Korean folk medicine for colds.[2]

Brands cite antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, with extract typically at 1 to 3 percent in products marketed for redness, pores, sebum and hydration, popular in K-beauty since the 2010s.[1][2] Cell studies report flavonoids such as quercitrin reducing inflammatory mediators and antibacterial activity against Cutibacterium acnes; a small toner study is reported to show reduced sebum and improved moisture at 8 weeks, with few design details available.[2]

Laboratory studies and reviews have examined anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and antiviral activities of the plant, including activity against influenza and herpes simplex virus in cell systems.[3][4][5] A review of anti-inflammatory and oxidative-stress effects was published in 2018.[5]

Patch testing before topical use is suggested in one source because of reported contact dermatitis in sensitive users.[2] In a rat 28-day study high oral doses caused liver and kidney toxicity, and China suspended intravenous use of herbal injections in 2006 after severe reactions including anaphylaxis.[2] Aristolactam components have raised kidney-cell toxicity concerns in vitro.[2]

No controlled clinical trials of Houttuynia cordata for skin appearance were found in the registries and literature reviewed. Registered trials of products containing it address respiratory infection, dry eye and atopic dermatitis in herbal formulas (for example NCT02539277, NCT05455060), and cannot isolate its effect.[6][7]

timeline.event: China suspends intravenous use of Houttuynia injections after severe reactions.[2]
Chinese researchers study the plant against SARS.[1][3]
